meaning: The total market value of the money a fund is managing for all its investors on a given day.
why: It shows how large a fund is. Very small funds can be costlier to run and may be closed down; very large funds can find it harder to trade in smaller companies.
how: Compare AUM only between similar funds. A big AUM says nothing about whether the fund will do well.
formula: AUM = Market value of all holdings + cash − liabilities
finlit: FinLit does not show AUM yet. AMFI publishes it in a separate monthly file, not in the daily NAV file.

meaning: The version of a mutual fund you buy straight from the fund house, with no distributor in between, so no distribution commission is paid out of the fund.
why: Because less is deducted every year, a Direct plan's NAV grows slightly faster than the Regular plan of the same fund holding the same investments.
how: Compare Direct with Direct and Regular with Regular. Their NAVs and returns differ even though the fund and its portfolio are the same.
finlit: On FinLit every scheme shows its plan, and the other plans of the same fund are linked on its page.

meaning: The version of a mutual fund bought through a distributor or advisor. A commission for them is paid out of the fund, so its yearly cost is higher than the Direct plan's.
why: The extra cost lowers the Regular plan's NAV growth against the Direct plan of the same fund, by about the difference in their expense ratios.
how: Compare Regular with Regular, and keep in mind what the extra cost pays for (advice or service).
finlit: On FinLit every scheme shows its plan, and the other plans of the same fund are linked on its page.

meaning: The choice under which a fund keeps all its earnings invested, so no money is paid out and the NAV rises as the investments grow.
why: With no payouts, the change in NAV tells the whole story of what the fund earned, so returns are simple to measure.
how: Growth and IDCW options of the same fund hold the same investments but have different NAVs; compare like with like.
finlit: FinLit works out returns, volatility and drawdown for Growth options from their NAV history.

meaning: The choice under which a fund pays out part of its value to you from time to time. It replaced the older name 'dividend option'. 'Payout' sends the money to you; 'reinvestment' buys more units with it.
why: Each payout is taken out of the NAV, so the NAV falls when it is paid. The payout is not extra profit; it is part of your own money coming back.
how: Never compare the NAV change of an IDCW option with a Growth option: the IDCW NAV is lower because of payouts, not because the fund did worse.
finlit: FinLit lists IDCW options with their own NAV but does not work out returns for them, since the payouts would be missing from a NAV-to-NAV change.

meaning: The group SEBI places a mutual fund scheme in according to what it invests in, such as Large Cap, Mid Cap, Liquid or Gilt. AMFI lists every scheme under its category.
why: Funds in the same category follow similar rules, so they are the fair ones to put side by side. Comparing a liquid fund with a small-cap fund is not meaningful.
how: Use the category to narrow the list before you compare returns or risk.
finlit: FinLit shows each scheme under the category AMFI files it in.

meaning: An open-ended fund takes in and pays out money every business day at the NAV. A closed-ended fund raises money once, runs for a fixed term and can be sold only on the stock exchange or when it matures. An interval fund opens only at set times.
why: It decides whether and when you can enter or leave. Many closed-ended and interval schemes have stopped publishing NAVs because their term ended.
how: Check the scheme type before assuming you can sell at the NAV on any day.
finlit: FinLit marks closed-ended and interval schemes from AMFI's headings and hides schemes that stopped publishing NAVs unless you ask to see them.

meaning: A fee a fund charges, as a percentage of the amount, if you sell units within a stated period after buying them.
why: It reduces what you receive if you leave early, and it differs from fund to fund.
how: Read the fund's offer document for its exit load and period before you invest.
formula: Amount received = Units × NAV × (1 − Exit load %)
finlit: FinLit does not show exit loads yet; they are not in AMFI's NAV file.

meaning: The company that sets up and manages mutual fund schemes, called an asset management company (AMC), for example Axis Mutual Fund or HDFC Mutual Fund.
why: The same fund house runs many schemes. Knowing it tells you who manages the money and which other schemes it runs.
how: A fund house is a company, and schemes of one fund house can behave very differently from each other.
finlit: FinLit groups schemes by the fund house name AMFI gives.

meaning: How much a fund's NAV changed from a date in the past (one month, six months, one year...) up to the latest NAV.
why: It is the standard way to read a fund's past results over different time spans, all ending today.
how: Trailing returns depend on the day you stop counting, so a fund can look different a month later. Past results do not guarantee future results.
formula:
1-year return = (Latest NAV ÷ NAV one year earlier) − 1
For more than a year: (Latest NAV ÷ Start NAV)^(365 ÷ days between the two NAV dates) − 1
finlit: FinLit takes the start NAV from the latest NAV on or before the start date and states for every figure whether it is a plain change (up to 1 year) or a yearly rate (3 and 5 years).

meaning: International Securities Identification Number: a 12-character code that identifies one security, or one plan and option of a mutual fund, worldwide.
why: Different plans and options of a fund have different ISINs and NAVs. The ISIN is the exact way to be sure you mean the same one.
how: Match the ISIN, not just the fund name, when you compare data from two places.
finlit: FinLit shows the ISIN AMFI gives for each scheme's growth units.

meaning: The Association of Mutual Funds in India, the industry body whose public files publish every scheme's daily NAV.
why: Its NAV files are the official source of mutual fund NAVs in India.
how: AMFI publishes NAVs after fund houses declare them; some funds report late in the evening.
finlit: FinLit builds its mutual fund pages from AMFI's own NAV files and shows the data date on every page.
aliases: Association of Mutual Funds in India
